title: Hardware signal and sampling yield across circuit depth
caption: (a) Saved raw and single-excitation-post-selected receiver energy fractions for the healthy 15-qubit unary wave experiment on ibm_marrakesh, with the independently saved exact reference (dotted line). FakeKingston post-selected simulation results are a different-device noise-model comparison. (b) Fraction of shots retained by post-selection. There is one hardware job and one circuit result per condition, with 4,000 shots per circuit; displayed error bars are the saved estimated binomial sampling standard errors, not between-job variation. All six 4,000-shot count dictionaries reproduce the saved aggregates. Supplied IBM job metadata report 9 seconds of charged QPU usage (6.62 seconds of circuit execution); independent hardware repeats remain absent. These results concern wave energy, not the separate signed-pressure inversion pipeline. Raw denotes the probability of the receiver-only bitstring (all other qubits zero), not the marginal probability that the receiver qubit is one.

title: Post-selection reduces observed error; additional ZNE is inconclusive
caption: (a) Raw, post-selected and post-selected plus linear zero-noise-extrapolated (ZNE) estimates for the healthy eight-step hardware circuit. The reference is 0.10403379. Raw and post-selected estimates share the same 4,000 original shots. ZNE uses a further 4,000 shots at fold factor three: E(0) = 1.5 E(1) - 0.5 E(3). Its standard error is propagated assuming independent circuit samples. Error bars show one estimated sampling standard error; they exclude calibration drift and model bias. Post-selection reduces the point-estimate absolute error by 74.95% in this one job. ZNE slightly increases absolute error and substantially increases uncertainty. (b) Only 652 and 60 shots survive at folds one and three, respectively. The folded estimate contains just five receiver-target events among its 60 retained shots; normal-approximation errors should not be treated as a rigorous coverage guarantee. Raw denotes the probability of the receiver-only bitstring (all other qubits zero), not the marginal probability that the receiver qubit is one.

title: Pressure simulations expose noise and finite-shot sensitivity
caption: (a) Relative L2 pressure error versus the exact reduced discrete wave model. Bars show the error of the mean trace over three forward repeats; black dots show errors of individual repeats. These are different statistics. The ideal mean trace error is 0.583%, but individual repeat errors are 1.076%, 1.333% and 1.565%, all above the 1% target. Noisy mean-trace error is 8.854%. The fixed-map pilot uses parameters (1, 1.1), two sources, two receivers, two time points and 8,192 shots per circuit. Noise is generic 0.1% depolarization, not a calibrated IBM model. (b) Final second-cell speed ratios after two optimizer updates, one run per condition, for initial-pressure and bipolar-pressure-rate inputs. Synthetic observations were generated by the same exact discrete model. Observations and inverse-problem signatures match across classical, ideal and noisy methods. Raw pilot counts reproduce the pressure traces; saved reconstructions match the histories. Source hashes were checked. This verifies saved-data consistency, not an independent solver rerun, convergence or clinical validation.

title: SA and SQA comparison on the same fixed-map forward task
caption: (a) Bars show relative L2 error of the mean pressure trace over three repeats; dots show each repeat error. (b) Bars show mean CPU wall time per forward run; dots show each measured time. Wall times include solver construction and recording work, and runs may contend for CPU resources (two workers). Simulated annealing (SA) is the classical control. Simulated quantum annealing (SQA) is a classical CPU path-integral simulation of a transverse-field model using D-Wave samplers; no annealing hardware or IBM annealer was used. Both solve the shared fixed-map 1D forward problem with the same configured annealing budgets: 6-bit encoding, 3 refinements, 16 reads and 200 sweeps. Both missed the rule requiring every repeat to have at most 1% error. SQA took 10.08 times longer on average in this test. This is a simulator-runtime observation, not a quantum hardware speed comparison. Arithmetic, acquisition signatures and source snapshots were checked against the supplied archives; no independent rerun was performed.

title: Exploratory pressure pilots motivate gate twirling
caption: (a) Raw pressure estimates on ibm_kingston versus the noiseless circuit reference, with approximate shot-only standard errors. The same 12 saved ISA circuits (eight wave circuits and four readout calibrations), physical qubits and 1,024 shots per circuit were used in both jobs. Only gate twirling changed: off versus 32 randomizations with 32 shots each. All circuits matched the ideal reference in an exact four-active-qubit statevector check. (b) RMSE across the eight pressure observations, before and after assignment readout correction. Twirling lowered raw RMSE from 0.800 to 0.149 Pa in this exploratory comparison; readout correction increased RMSE in both jobs. Each job used 6 charged QPU seconds. These pilots motivated the separate three-pair follow-up and are excluded from its summaries. One job per condition cannot isolate drift or establish repeatability. Shot-only bars do not include randomization variability, gate bias or cross-job drift.

title: Gate twirling lowers pressure error in three paired hardware repeats
caption: (a) Mean raw pressure estimates across three jobs per arm; error bars show sample standard deviation across jobs, not shot standard error or a confidence interval. The diagonal is the noiseless circuit prediction. (b) Each line connects one prespecified pair; short black bars show arm means. Mean RMSE decreased from 0.664 to 0.148 Pa, a mean paired RMSE reduction of 0.516 Pa. The 77.76% relative reduction is calculated as 1 minus twirled mean divided by untwirled mean; it is not the mean pairwise percentage. Pairwise reductions were 65.00%, 80.52% and 81.93%. All six jobs used the identical 12 saved ISA circuits on ibm_kingston, four active physical qubits (81, 82, 83, 96), and 4,096 shots per circuit. Gate-twirled jobs used 32 randomizations with 128 shots each. Pair orders were untwirled/twirled, twirled/untwirled, untwirled/twirled. Readout calibration passed in all jobs, but correction worsened all six RMSEs; corrected arm means were 0.684 and 0.162 Pa. No dynamical decoupling, measurement twirling or quantum error correction was used. The six jobs used 99 charged QPU seconds; including the two exploratory pilots, usage for this signed-pressure campaign was 111 seconds, separate from the earlier Marrakesh experiment. All 72 count dictionaries and derived pressure reports were checked. This short single-backend campaign has only three pairs and visible control drift; it establishes observed improvement at this test case, not general superiority, a clinical result or computational speedup.

title: Recorded CPU runtime for the shared reduced pilot task
caption: Dots show individual recorded CPU wall times on a logarithmic axis; short horizontal marks show means. Classical exact pools six measurements from the two gate-benchmark control blocks; each other method has three repeats. Mean times are 2.575 ms (classical), 0.1246 s (ideal Aer), 0.1738 s (noisy Aer), 0.1878 s (SA) and 1.8927 s (SQA). Gate timings include circuit construction, transpilation, simulation and count recording; classical timings include solver construction and prediction; annealing timings include solver and recording with possible contention between two workers. The physical task is shared, but achieved accuracy and timing boundaries differ. These are configured-workflow measurements, not time-to-equal-accuracy, a hardware comparison or an observed quantum speedup. Classical CPU simulation of a quantum method need not predict its future quantum hardware runtime.
